# Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete

> Official website for iOS app 6754815949 by Mohamed Elatabany.

Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete is an iPhone photo-cleanup app by Mohamed Elatabany for iOS 17 or later. It offers a personal cleanup plan, duplicate and similar-photo review, screenshot and large-video review, and swipe-to-keep or mark-for-removal controls. Photo analysis happens on your device; photos are not uploaded for scanning. Start with a one-time free allowance; Pro unlocks unlimited swipes and advanced cleanup tools, with subscription and one-time purchase options depending on availability. Rated 5 stars on the US App Store, checked October 4, 2026.

Canonical App Store listing: https://apps.apple.com/app/id6754815949

Questions, answered.
What is Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete?
It is an iPhone photo-cleanup app by Mohamed Elatabany. It offers a personal cleanup plan, duplicate and similar-photo review, screenshot and large-video review, and swipe controls. You review marked items before confirming deletion.
Does it upload my photos for analysis?
Photo analysis runs on your iPhone; photos are not uploaded for scanning or cleanup decisions. Apple and RevenueCat process purchase services. Apple Photos may download iCloud media when requested.
Is Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete free?
It starts with a one-time free allowance. Optional Pro purchases unlock unlimited swipes and advanced cleanup tools. Current purchase options and terms appear in the app.
What happens when I delete an iCloud photo?
When iCloud Photos is enabled, deleting an item also removes it from other devices using that synced library. Check your selections and keep a separate backup of irreplaceable media.

### About Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete
https://swipeanddelete.app/about.html
Home
About Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete
Updated October 2026
Made by Mohamed Elatabany to help you make deliberate choices about your photo library.
A plan, not a rush.
Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete combines a personal cleanup plan with focused review sessions. Its purpose is to help you find unnecessary photos and videos while keeping the decisions in your hands.
The App Store developer is Mohamed Elatabany. View my public GitHub profile or verify this app's developer on the App Store.
How we write guides.
Guides explain Apple's built-in options first and link to Apple documentation. App descriptions are checked against the app's code and live App Store listing. Comparisons use competitors' own current listings and documentation. We identify estimates, explain limitations, and avoid invented ratings or claims of guaranteed results.
These guides are published by the developer of a photo-cleanup app; comparisons therefore have a commercial interest. Choose the built-in Photos app if it solves your problem.
Menu locations change between iOS versions. Check the date on each guide, and send a correction if something needs updating.

### Support for Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete
https://swipeanddelete.app/support.html
Home
Support for Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete
Updated October 2026
Need a hand? Email atabany.apps@gmail.com.
Include your iPhone model, iOS version, app version, and what happened. Please avoid sending private photos or purchase credentials.
Photo access
The app can only review the photos you allow it to access. Use iPhone Settings to find the app's Photos permission and adjust access. Limited access means only selected photos are available for review.
Recover a photo
Before confirming deletion, restore marked items from the in-app Trash Bin. After deleting, check Recently Deleted in Apple's Photos app. Apple normally keeps deleted items there for 30 days, unless you permanently remove them earlier. When iCloud Photos is enabled, deletion syncs to your other devices.
Apple's deletion and recovery instructions
Purchases and subscriptions
Use Restore Purchases on the paywall with the Apple Account that made the purchase. To manage a subscription, open Settings, tap your name, then Subscriptions. Apple handles billing and refund requests.
Manage or cancel a subscription · Request a refund from Apple
Website corrections
Include the page URL and the detail that appears incorrect. The maker reviews corrections; no response time is guaranteed.

### Privacy information
https://swipeanddelete.app/privacy.html
Home
Privacy information
Updated October 2026
Photo analysis happens on your device. Your photos are not uploaded for scanning or cleanup decisions.
Your Photos library
The app uses Apple's Photos permission to access your authorized library. Duplicate detection, similar-photo review, and cleanup decisions are processed on your device. Photos stored in iCloud may be downloaded by Apple's Photos services when you request them; that is separate from uploading photos to our servers.
Review progress and preferences are stored locally. The app also stores its free-allowance usage locally, including in Keychain. Revoking Photos access prevents further access to your library through the app.
Purchase services
Apple processes in-app purchases. The app uses RevenueCat to manage purchase status and Pro entitlements. Purchase records, app-user identifiers, and relevant device or usage information may be processed by those services to manage entitlements and operate their services. On-device photo analysis does not mean that no information ever leaves the device.
RevenueCat privacy policy · Apple privacy policy
This website and the planner
This website does not include advertising, third-party fonts, or analytics scripts. The cleanup planner calculates estimates in your browser and does not send your entries or photos to us. GitHub Pages hosts the website and can process standard request information needed to serve it.
Download links contain Apple's campaign parameters so aggregate downloads can be attributed in App Store Connect when Apple reports them. The links do not contain your photo data.
Current policy and contact
This page explains the implementation checked on October 4, 2026. The privacy policy currently linked from the App Store remains available. If you email support, your message and contact details are used to respond. Contact atabany.apps@gmail.com with privacy questions or requests to access or delete information held by the developer. Local review data can be reset in the app; purchase-allowance records may persist in Keychain. Apple and RevenueCat maintain their own records under their policies.

### Photo Cleanup Planner — Estimate Storage to Review
https://swipeanddelete.app/cleanup-planner.html
Home
Photo Cleanup Planner — Estimate Storage to Review
Updated October 2026
Estimate the space in unwanted photos, screenshots, and videos, then see which group is worth reviewing first. Everything runs in your browser; no library access or uploads.
Unwanted photos, excluding screenshotsAverage photo size (MB)Old screenshotsAverage screenshot size (MB)Unwanted videosAverage video size (MB)
2.4 GB in this example
Videos account for 2 GB, photos for 0.3 GB, and screenshots for 0.1 GB.
Use the reference table below: multiply each count by its average size, add the results, then divide MB by 1,000 for decimal GB.
The math, without the guesswork.
Estimated GB = (photo count × average photo MB + screenshot count × average screenshot MB + video count × average video MB) ÷ 1,000. Categories must not overlap. The default sizes are illustrative inputs, not measured averages.
Reference examples with explicit assumptions
| Group | Count | Assumed size each | Total file size
| Photos | 100 | 3 MB | 0.3 GB
| Screenshots | 100 | 1 MB | 0.1 GB
| Videos | 10 | 200 MB | 2 GB
| Combined, no overlap | 210 | Mixed | 2.4 GB
Use sizes from your own library.
Open a photo or video in Photos and open its information view to inspect its details. Sample a few unwanted items rather than assuming every file is the same size. Videos vary dramatically with duration, resolution, frame rate and recording format.
Check Settings → General → iPhone Storage before and after cleanup. With Optimize iPhone Storage enabled, full originals may already live in iCloud, so deleting total file bytes may free much less local space. Recently Deleted can also retain removed items. Keep its recovery window when you can; permanently deleting an item removes that safety net.
Apple: check device storage · Apple: manage photo storage
Turn the estimate into a safe plan.
Start with the group contributing the most file bytes.
Review items individually and keep anything irreplaceable.
Check iCloud syncing and your separate backup before confirming deletion.
Check actual iPhone storage after Photos has processed the change.
The planner never scans or deletes your photos. For focused review on your iPhone, Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete offers a personal cleanup plan, similar-photo comparisons, and an in-app Trash Bin for review before confirmed deletion.

### How to Delete Duplicate Photos on iPhone
https://swipeanddelete.app/delete-duplicate-photos-iphone.html
Home / Guides
How to delete duplicate photos on iPhone
Open the Duplicates collection in Apple Photos, review a set, and use Merge to keep one combined copy. The route depends on your iOS version, and photos that merely look alike may need a separate manual review.
By Mohamed Elatabany · Updated October 2026 · Suggest a correction
On this page
Start with Apple Photos
If Duplicates is missing
Check what a copy means to you
Handle similar shots separately
Use a focused review when grouping is not enough
Finish with a check, not a target
Sources and further reading
Start with Apple Photos
Use the built-in duplicate tool before adding another app. On iOS 17, open Photos, tap Albums, and find Duplicates under Utilities. On iOS 18, find Utilities on the main Photos screen, then Duplicates. On iOS 26, tap Collections, then Utilities, then Duplicates. Tap Merge beside a set and confirm the number of items. These routes are documented in Apple’s version-specific guides below.
Test one obvious pair first. Choose a copy you recognize and look at both images at a comfortable size. This small trial lets you understand the result before tackling the rest of the library. There is no need to treat every proposed pair as a decision you must make today. A short first pass is easier to check than a large, rushed batch.
If Duplicates is missing
An absent collection does not tell you how tidy the entire camera roll is. Apple says duplicate discovery first requires indexing and detection. Leave the iPhone locked and connected to power; depending on library size and background activity, detection may take a few days. When Photos has no detected duplicates, the collection does not appear. The Apple troubleshooting link explains these conditions.
While you wait, do something that does not depend on detection: review a familiar trip, old screenshots, or a small collection of repeated downloads. Resist repeatedly adding copies just to test the tool. That creates more clutter and makes the eventual results harder to interpret. Make a note of the originals you want to compare later, then return after the phone has had an uninterrupted charging period.
Check what a copy means to you
A picture can have a purpose beyond its visible subject. You may have an original for future editing, a crop for a profile, and an annotated copy for explaining something to a friend. Before removing a version, ask whether its edits or context are still useful. If you cannot answer confidently, leave that set for a later session. Freeing space is useful only when the remaining collection serves you better.
For an easy decision, start with an accidental repeat download. For a difficult decision, compare the whole frame: text, expressions, edges, and anything added to the image. Avoid deciding from a tiny thumbnail. You are choosing what belongs in your library, not trying to meet a deletion quota. A copy worth keeping can remain even if an app puts it beside another one.
Handle similar shots separately
Two pictures from the same moment may be different photographs. A child’s expression, a moving pet, or a person entering the background can make one frame meaningful. The word similar is a request to compare, not an instruction to delete. Keep both when they tell different parts of the story. For a holiday landscape, you may prefer one broad view and one closer detail rather than a single winner.
An efficient order is to identify your favorite first, then assess the remaining frames against it. If you are preparing an album, think about how the pictures work together. Five versions of the same pose may be unnecessary, while two complementary images may be exactly right. The separate similar versus duplicate guide gives a more detailed decision process.
Use a focused review when grouping is not enough
Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete provides a swipe-and-review workflow for photo-library cleanup. Use a small, recognizable category for your first session. Make your keep-or-remove choices deliberately, then inspect the selections before confirming deletion. If a group includes something uncertain, keep it and move on. Review is the useful part of the workflow; a larger selected count is not a better result by itself.
Before starting, decide on one rule such as “keep the best family portrait and every genuinely different expression.” That rule prevents inconsistent decisions halfway through a group. Stop when you no longer feel attentive. A repeatable ten-minute session is often more practical than committing to clean an entire library at once. The app’s role is to organize the work you choose to do.
Finish with a check, not a target
After your pass, open the events you touched and confirm that the pictures you wanted are still there. Check a few important examples rather than relying only on a count. Write down what worked: perhaps repeated downloads were simple, while edited photos needed more attention. Next time, start with the easier category and leave enough time for the difficult decisions.
Before any cleanup, remember that iCloud Photos synchronizes deletions. Do not treat another synced device as an independent backup. Read the iCloud deletion guide if your goal is to free local space while preserving originals elsewhere. Avoid immediately making every deletion permanent; give yourself time to spot a mistaken choice. The goal is a library you can navigate with confidence.
Sources and further reading
Apple: Merge duplicates, iOS 17
Apple: Merge duplicates, iOS 18
Apple: Merge duplicates, iOS 26
Apple: Duplicates album missing
Apple: Delete photos on iPhone or iPad
Questions, answered.
Does Apple Photos find every similar picture?
Do not assume that a Duplicates result covers every lookalike frame. Use it for the sets Apple detects, then compare different shots of the same subject separately.
Why can’t I see Duplicates?
Apple requires time to index and detect duplicates while the phone is locked and on power. The collection is absent when no duplicates are detected.
Should I delete every extra photo in a group?
Keep versions with a separate purpose, edit or moment. A useful original and an annotated copy can both belong in your library.

### Similar vs Duplicate Photos: What Should You Keep?
https://swipeanddelete.app/similar-vs-duplicate-photos.html
Home / Guides
Similar versus duplicate photos: a practical keep checklist
Duplicate copies repeat an image, while similar photos can show different frames, expressions or edits. Start with Apple Photos’ detected duplicate sets, then make a deliberate choice about lookalikes instead of treating every similar image as disposable.
By Mohamed Elatabany · Updated October 2026 · Suggest a correction
On this page
Use the built-in duplicate review first
Three situations that look the same in a grid
Pick a keeper using five questions
When keeping more than one is the right choice
Make recommendations a starting point
An example that avoids a rushed choice
Sources and further reading
Use the built-in duplicate review first
Apple Photos gives you a starting point for detected copies. On iOS 17, look in Albums under Utilities; on iOS 18, find Utilities on the Photos screen; on iOS 26, open Collections and then Utilities. Open Duplicates and examine a set before choosing Merge. The version-specific Apple references below describe the routes. Once you have reviewed those sets, return to the events with several different shots.
A two-pass approach keeps different tasks clear. The first pass handles repeated copies. The second pass handles personal selection, such as deciding which portrait belongs in a family album. You do not need the same rule for both passes. An accidental duplicate download is a simple housekeeping choice. Picking between two smiles is an editorial choice that depends on what you value.
Three situations that look the same in a grid
Imagine three adjacent thumbnails of a dog. The first and second are repeated saves of the same picture. The third was taken a second later, when the dog looked toward the camera. The third may look nearly identical at thumbnail size, yet it can be the one you want to keep. A familiar subject and a familiar background do not prove that nothing changed.
An edited copy adds a third case. You might have a full image, a square crop and a version with a label. Decide what each version is for. If the crop is still your profile image, it has a reason to stay. If an annotation records an important measurement, visual repetition does not make it useless. Read the contents rather than judging only the outline or color.
Pick a keeper using five questions
First ask whether the picture matters at all. If it does, check the expression, the clarity of the subject, the framing, the important details, and the purpose of that version. There is no universal order. For a group portrait, everyone’s expression may matter most. For a receipt, legible text matters more than beautiful framing. For a pet, an unusual gesture can outweigh perfect sharpness.
Compare at a size that lets you inspect the detail you care about. If an image is destined for a small contact avatar, evaluate the face and crop. If it is destined for a large print, inspect the original more carefully. Write down your priority before a long session so that the next group receives the same attention. Keep uncertainty out of the deletion selection.
When keeping more than one is the right choice
A sequence can tell a story that a single image cannot. Consider a birthday candle before and after it is blown out, or a landscape in changing light. You may want one photograph for an album and another because it includes a relative who rarely appears in pictures. These are different reasons to keep a frame, even when the scene is broadly similar.
Try selecting a small story rather than a single best shot. One establishing image, one close detail and one candid moment can feel more complete than ten almost matching portraits. If two frames genuinely add nothing different, removing the less useful one is reasonable. If they preserve separate memories, keep them. The aim is to make your choices intentional, not to force a fixed number per event.
Make recommendations a starting point
A cleanup app can arrange candidates so you spend less time finding them. Your role is still to check what matters in each group. In Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete, work through a focused category and review your chosen removals before confirming. Use the full picture when a tiny preview leaves doubt. Photo analysis is performed on your device; a suggested group does not replace your judgment.
Begin with an event you remember well. That lets you spot a meaningful alternate expression or an edited version quickly. After a few decisions, pause and look at your keep choices together. Do they retain the story you intended? If you are uncertain about a particular frame, leave it in the library. You can revisit a small deferred group when you have more context or a larger screen.
An example that avoids a rushed choice
Suppose you have twelve pictures from a beach walk. Four repeat a downloaded image, five are attempts at the same portrait, and three capture different parts of the walk. Review the repeated saves first. Then compare the portraits: eyes, expression, horizon and whether anything important is cropped. Finally, assess the three separate moments as a group. You may reasonably keep all three.
The useful result is an understandable set, not a promised storage gain. Record the decision rule that helped you most and reuse it for the next event. If you are tidying to save space, inspect large videos separately; a photo count alone does not tell you what will make the largest difference. Before deleting, consider your sync and backup arrangement using the linked iCloud guide.
Sources and further reading
Apple: Merge duplicates, iOS 17
Apple: Merge duplicates, iOS 18
Apple: Merge duplicates, iOS 26
Apple: View photo and video information
Questions, answered.
Is a burst a duplicate?
A burst can contain different frames of a moving subject. Inspect the expression, action and framing before choosing which frames to keep.
Can I trust a suggested best photo?
Treat it as a suggestion. Your favorite may depend on a person, detail or memory that an automated comparison cannot decide for you.
Should I keep original and edited versions?
Keep both when they serve separate purposes. If the edited version is obsolete and you are sure you will not need it, it can be a reasonable removal candidate.

### How to Delete Screenshots on iPhone
https://swipeanddelete.app/delete-screenshots-iphone.html
Home / Guides
How to delete screenshots without losing useful information
Find Screenshots in Apple Photos, select the captures you no longer need, and confirm deletion. Review tickets, receipts, reference numbers and other useful information before treating a whole screenshot collection as clutter.
By Mohamed Elatabany · Updated October 2026 · Suggest a correction
On this page
Start in the Screenshots collection
Separate information from temporary reminders
Use a three-pile decision
Be deliberate with sensitive captures
Use a focused screenshot session
Keep the next backlog small
Sources and further reading
Start in the Screenshots collection
In Apple Photos, find Screenshots within the media-type collections. On iOS 17 these appear in Albums; on iOS 18 they are on the main Photos screen; on iOS 26 start in Collections. Collection placement may vary with your layout. Open Screenshots, use Select to choose only the captures you have reviewed, then use the trash control and confirm. Start with a short visible batch.
Before selecting anything, choose a scope: old shopping research, completed travel plans, or captures from a particular month. That scope is more useful than a blanket rule about age. An old receipt may matter, while yesterday’s throwaway comparison may already be irrelevant. If you have hundreds of captures, do not start by assuming they all have the same purpose. Break the work into recognizable topics.
Separate information from temporary reminders
Screenshots often act as a second inbox. A confirmation page, a useful recipe, a reference number and a funny message may all sit together. For each capture, ask whether you need the picture itself, the information inside it, or neither. If the information still matters, decide where you would naturally look for it later. A travel document belongs with the rest of that trip’s documents.
Choose a way to retain important information before removing its screenshot. For example, save the original document, record the reference in your notes, or keep the capture until the event has passed. Verify that the retained version is readable and complete. Do not substitute a partial number or a cropped preview for the full information you actually need. This is a workflow recommendation, not a claim that every screenshot should be moved elsewhere.
Use a three-pile decision
Give yourself three outcomes: keep, remove and revisit. Keep active tickets, ongoing work references and sentimental captures. Remove material you recognize as finished or unnecessary. Revisit anything whose purpose you cannot remember quickly. The third outcome helps you make progress without converting uncertainty into deletion. You can return to that group after checking your calendar or asking yourself what project it belonged to.
An example: a completed furniture search leaves several nearly matching product captures. Keep the purchase confirmation if it remains useful. Remove rejected options you know you will not revisit. Leave an unfamiliar warranty screen until you have checked whether it belongs to the item you bought. A cleanup session feels more reliable when the reasoning stays connected to real tasks rather than a general “old means bad” rule.
Be deliberate with sensitive captures
A screenshot may contain more private information than the thumbnail reveals. Check captures of accounts, identity documents, conversations and work material carefully. If you retain a sensitive capture, consider where it belongs and who can access that location. If you no longer need it, review the deletion carefully. Avoid uploading screenshots to an unfamiliar web tool just to obtain a cleanup recommendation.
For this task, a readable local review is enough. Enlarge any text that influences your decision and verify whether the whole capture is relevant. A useful detail near the bottom of a long screenshot is easy to miss. Conversely, a capture of a page you can easily reopen may be less useful than an actual document. Make that distinction one item at a time when the consequences matter.
Use a focused screenshot session
Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete offers screenshot review as part of its photo-library workflow. Pick that category when you want to work through captures without bouncing between unrelated photos. Keep choices simple and review the selected removals before confirming. If you notice that you are guessing about what an image contains, stop and open it more carefully. A swipe is a convenient decision gesture, not a reason to skip reading.
Try a short session around one completed task. Keeping the context consistent makes decisions easier: all the captures relate to the same trip or purchase rather than years of unrelated reminders. After the session, inspect your remaining references. If the collection now contains only what you can explain, it is easier to maintain. The built-in Photos approach remains a good option when your batch is already small.
Keep the next backlog small
After a booking, delivery or finished project, review its captures while the purpose is fresh. Before taking a new screenshot, ask what you expect it to do: remember a link, preserve a document, or record something temporary. Choosing a destination at capture time can reduce the later work. The point is not to eliminate screenshots; it is to keep them useful and findable.
Use a recurring personal habit such as checking captures after travel rather than aiming for an empty collection. For storage concerns, compare the result with actual device storage instead of promising savings from an image count. If the phone is still full, review large videos next. Before a wider cleanup, read about iCloud deletion so your expectation matches your sync settings.
Sources and further reading

Apple: Find screenshots, iOS 26

Questions, answered.
Should I delete all screenshots at once?
Only if you have reviewed them and are sure none are useful. Tickets, receipts, account details and work references deserve a closer look.
Does removing screenshots remove my regular photos?
Selecting captures in a screenshot collection scopes your choices to those items. Still inspect the selection and confirmation before accepting it.
How do I keep screenshots under control?
Review captures when the task that created them ends. Save necessary information somewhere you can find it, and defer unclear items instead of guessing.

### How to Find Large Videos on iPhone
https://swipeanddelete.app/find-large-videos-iphone.html
Home / Guides
How to find and review large videos on iPhone
Check Settings → General → iPhone Storage, then open videos in Photos and swipe up or tap Info to inspect file details. Prioritize videos by their actual size and usefulness rather than guessing from how many thumbnails you see.
By Mohamed Elatabany · Updated October 2026 · Suggest a correction
On this page
Check where the space is going first
Inspect the individual files
Watch before you choose
Verify separate copies when preserving originals
Use the app for a focused review
Make future recordings easier to manage
Sources and further reading
Check where the space is going first
Open iPhone Storage and let the usage view load before deciding that photos are the problem. The useful question is which category deserves your attention. A photo-library cleanup is a sensible project when your saved media is substantial. If another app accounts for most of the usage, reviewing hundreds of pictures may do little for the immediate concern. Let the actual storage view set your next task.
Write down the available space before you begin, along with the goal: enough room for a recording, an update, or daily use. This is a baseline for your own comparison, not a promise of a particular result. Avoid turning a rough estimate into a precise deadline. Your device can have other activity during the session, so treat a later reading as context rather than a controlled experiment.
Inspect the individual files
Find the Videos media-type collection in Photos and open a candidate. Swipe up or use Info to view details such as file size. Apple’s information guide documents that view. Start with clips you remember being long or no longer useful, but confirm the size before making assumptions. The visible length, resolution and contents help you understand a file; the number of clips by itself does not.
For a small library, write a short candidate list with the event, approximate size and keep-or-review decision. This avoids jumping between unrelated recordings. For a large library, focus first on an obvious group such as obsolete screen recordings or repeated attempts at a demonstration. You are looking for a manageable set of decisions, not inspecting every video before doing anything useful.
Watch before you choose
Play important candidates, including the middle and ending when appropriate. A recording can begin with an uninteresting setup and end with the only good view of a meaningful moment. Listen when the audio might matter. A shaky video may preserve a person’s voice, a performance or a useful explanation. The best deletion candidate is the one you know you no longer need, not automatically the biggest file.
Choose different rules for different kinds of recording. For work demonstrations, keep the final useful version and assess failed attempts. For family moments, consider whether shorter alternatives actually preserve the same event. For temporary tutorials, check whether the recording is still your only reference. When the rule is clear, review becomes faster without depending on indiscriminate selection or a promised amount of reclaimed space.
Verify separate copies when preserving originals
If you plan to remove a video after saving it elsewhere, check the copy before deletion. Open it at the destination, watch enough to confirm it is complete, and make sure you know how to find it again. Merely seeing a filename is not a complete verification. For a particularly important recording, give the copy check its own session instead of doing it while rushing through removals.
Consider who is responsible for the copy and whether the destination has its own retention policy. A file shared with someone else may be convenient without being a dependable personal archive. Write down the location of the recording and the reason you chose it. If you have not confirmed a copy you trust, keep the original candidate until you can. Extra review time is reasonable for an irreplaceable moment.
Use the app for a focused review
Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete includes large-video review with file details. Use it to identify candidates and make deliberate choices about what belongs in your library. Review the selected items before confirming deletion. Keep any recording whose contents or copy status you have not checked. This app’s role here is media review and cleanup; do not expect it to clear system files or other apps’ caches.
Build a short list around one purpose, such as removing obsolete screen recordings. Once that list is done, stop and reassess your storage need. If you already have sufficient room, there is no reason to continue removing meaningful videos just because more candidates remain. A useful workflow has a stopping condition that follows your goal. The camera roll plan helps define bounded sessions.
Make future recordings easier to manage
Before recording a long event, decide what you actually need to capture and where the result will live. Afterward, review accidental starts, abandoned attempts and redundant takes while you remember them. A clear name or note about the event can also make future decisions easier. The habit matters more than making every recording as short as possible; some moments deserve the whole clip.
When checking the outcome, give device storage time to update and separate your review decisions from final removal. With iCloud Photos enabled, deletion synchronizes rather than preserving an untouched cloud original. Read the iCloud safety guide before relying on a synced copy. The most useful result is enough room for your next task while the recordings you care about remain accessible.

Open the video, then swipe up or tap Info. Apple documents file size among the metadata details available in Photos.
Is the longest video always the largest?
Do not assume so. Check actual file details before ranking candidates, and decide usefulness separately from size.
Does this app compress my videos?
This guide describes video review and deletion. Compression is not a feature promised by Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete on this site.

### Delete Photos Safely with iCloud Photos
https://swipeanddelete.app/icloud-photo-deletion.html
Home / Guides
How to delete safely when you use iCloud Photos
With iCloud Photos enabled, deleting a photo on your iPhone also deletes it from the synchronized library on your other devices. If your aim is to save local space while retaining your originals, check Optimize iPhone Storage before deleting anything.
By Mohamed Elatabany · Updated October 2026 · Suggest a correction
On this page
Start with the built-in storage option
Treat synchronization differently from an archive
Verify the files you want to preserve
Use a small, recognizable cleanup batch
Understand the recovery boundary
Keep the cleanup workflow connected to this decision
Sources and further reading
Start with the built-in storage option
For iOS 17, 18 and 26, open Settings, your name, iCloud, then Photos. Check Sync this iPhone and Optimize iPhone Storage. Apple describes optimization as keeping full-resolution originals in iCloud and smaller local versions as needed. Allow time for the device to manage its local copies, and check your available iCloud storage before relying on that arrangement.
Choose the approach based on your actual goal. Wanting fewer items in the library is different from wanting the same library to occupy less local space. Write that goal down before changing anything. If the pictures themselves remain valuable, a smaller local footprint may be the task. If the library contains things you no longer want anywhere, deliberate deletion may be appropriate. These choices deserve different review sessions.
Treat synchronization differently from an archive
Apple explains that iCloud Photos keeps changes in step across your devices. A second device signed into the same synchronized library is therefore not an independent copy for the purpose of protecting a deletion. Do not infer safety just because the picture appears on both a phone and a tablet. Check what connects those views before assuming one can restore the other.
An archive decision starts with a question: where will this original remain after I make a change? Answer it with a location and a verification step, rather than the word cloud. Different services and folders can behave differently. If you cannot describe how the destination handles deletion, pause the removal and inspect it. This practical distinction avoids a common misunderstanding without requiring you to reorganize every storage service you use.
Verify the files you want to preserve
If you choose to keep a separate copy, open the exported material at the destination. Check several important photographs at full viewing size and play important videos. Confirm that a sequence contains the expected files, not only a preview or an incomplete transfer. Make sure you can locate the result without relying on a temporary notification or a recently opened list.
For an event you care about, keep a simple inventory: the date, destination and whether the copy was checked. The inventory does not need to be complicated. A short note that you can understand later is sufficient. If another person manages the destination, agree on what will be retained before removing your originals. A clear, verified copy plan is more useful than a vague assurance that something was uploaded.
Use a small, recognizable cleanup batch
Once your goal and copy arrangement are clear, choose a modest batch of media you definitely do not need. Completed shopping research or an obsolete screenshot is easier to assess than an unfamiliar family event. Inspect each item and confirm the selection before accepting deletion. Afterward, check the library views you use normally so the result matches your expectation.
Keep the first batch separate from your larger plan. If the outcome surprises you, stop and investigate before making more changes. This is particularly useful when you recently changed devices or enabled synchronization. You do not need to learn every iCloud setting during the same session in which you remove files. Understand the relevant behavior first, then resume your cleanup with a rule you can explain.
Understand the recovery boundary
Apple provides Recently Deleted for recovering photos and videos for 30 days unless they are permanently removed sooner. In iOS 26, open Photos, Collections, Utilities, then Recently Deleted and unlock the collection. Select the items and choose Recover. Earlier editions expose Recently Deleted under their Utilities area. Apple’s current deletion support article gives the available recovery and permanent-removal controls.
Use that recovery window as a chance to review a mistake, not as an excuse to make uncertain choices. Do not empty everything merely to make a counter look final. If you notice a missing image, inspect recovery promptly and check that it returns to the library. Shared libraries have extra ownership rules for permanent removal and recovery; consult Apple’s guide before managing another person’s contribution.
Keep the cleanup workflow connected to this decision
Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete helps you review photo-library clutter and confirm removals. It does not turn iCloud Photos into a separate archive, and an app selection cannot change what synchronization means. Use the workflow for media you genuinely want to remove, after resolving where your keepers belong. Photo analysis takes place on-device, which concerns scanning privacy rather than the retention behavior of iCloud.
For the next session, choose one narrow purpose and stop when it is complete. For example, remove screenshots from a finished trip while keeping photographs from that trip. If the phone still needs room, reassess the storage view and your optimization settings. The large-video guide can help prioritize actual media sizes, while the camera roll plan provides a repeatable review structure.
Sources and further reading
Apple: Manage photo and video storage
Apple: Set up and use iCloud Photos
Apple: Delete photos on iPhone or iPad
Questions, answered.
Can I delete from iPhone and keep the same synced iCloud photo?
With iCloud Photos enabled, deletion propagates across the synchronized library. Use Optimize iPhone Storage for a smaller local footprint while retaining cloud originals.
Is Optimize Storage a way to reduce iCloud usage?
It changes local storage management. Your full-resolution originals still occupy iCloud storage; reducing the cloud library is a different task.
Should I empty Recently Deleted immediately?
Only when you are certain about permanent removal. Apple’s recovery opportunity ends when items are permanently deleted, even if the usual window has not expired.

### A Simple Swipe Cleanup Plan for Your Camera Roll
https://swipeanddelete.app/swipe-photo-cleanup.html
Home / Guides
A simple swipe cleanup plan for your camera roll
Start with a small group in Apple Photos, decide what to keep, and review selected removals before confirming deletion. A swipe workflow can make repeated choices easier, especially when you define one category and a clear stopping point before starting.
By Mohamed Elatabany · Updated October 2026 · Suggest a correction
On this page
Try the built-in method on a small batch
Name the outcome before choosing photos
Use clear keep and remove rules
Use swipe choices in a bounded session
Separate selection from confirmation
Make maintenance easier than the first cleanup
Sources and further reading
Try the built-in method on a small batch
Open a familiar event or collection in Apple Photos. Use Select, choose the pictures you no longer need, and review the selection before using the trash control. You can do useful cleanup this way without adding an app. If the batch contains repeated copies, review the built-in Duplicates collection first; the duplicate guide explains the routes for iOS 17, 18 and 26.
The first batch is a practice session, not a race. Choose an event whose contents you understand and decide on a small endpoint, such as finishing that event or stopping after ten minutes. Observe where decisions become difficult. If you find yourself guessing about unknown pictures, change the scope to something clearer. A method works well when it helps you make reliable choices repeatedly.
Name the outcome before choosing photos
Choose one goal: remove temporary references, simplify a holiday album, or make room for a coming recording. Each suggests different candidates. Temporary references call for a task-based review. Album selection calls for looking at the story the pictures tell. A storage concern calls for checking actual usage and larger media, not simply choosing the biggest number of thumbnails you can remove.
Write one sentence that defines success. “I have kept the useful captures from this completed purchase” is specific. “My entire phone is clean” is too broad to guide a session. The smaller outcome also gives you permission to stop. If you need another session, you can choose it deliberately after checking what remains instead of continuing because the camera roll still contains thousands of pictures.
Use clear keep and remove rules
Keep irreplaceable memories, useful documents and photographs with a distinct purpose. Remove accidental saves, obsolete references and frames you have compared carefully and do not want. Leave ambiguous choices for later. These are starting rules to adapt, not automatic judgments about every file. A photograph that looks ordinary to someone else may matter because of who is in it or when it was taken.
For a group of portraits, pick a favorite and then ask whether another frame adds a genuinely different expression. For screenshots, ask whether the underlying task is complete. For videos, check contents before choosing. Switching rules from one category to another is reasonable; switching them randomly within one session creates confusion. Use the similar-photo checklist when an apparent duplicate is actually a different moment.
Use swipe choices in a bounded session
Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete uses right to keep and left to mark for removal. Choose a focused category or a short Quick Sweep session rather than beginning with the whole library. If you change your mind, undo your choice or restore an item in the in-app Trash Bin before confirming deletion. Photo analysis runs on your device; you still decide which candidates belong in the final selection.
Keep a comfortable pace. When you notice that several decisions have become guesses, pause. A brief break gives you a chance to see whether the next item actually fits the rule you chose. Convenience is helpful when it reduces repetitive navigation, but accuracy depends on attention. You can finish a smaller session today and return tomorrow; progress does not require an unbroken marathon.
Separate selection from confirmation
Treat the final review as its own step. Look through the chosen removals with your original goal in mind. Check any sensitive document, sentimental event or group of lookalike portraits closely. If you cannot explain why an item is selected, keep it. This final pass can catch a decision that made sense at speed but feels wrong once you see the group together.
Confirm only after the selections look right. Then revisit one or two important keeper groups in the library. A good session leaves the collection easier to understand and preserves the moments you intended. Avoid judging the experience solely by a claimed space estimate. If storage is the goal, compare with the device view afterward and remember that updates and other activity can affect what you see.
Make maintenance easier than the first cleanup
Tie future sessions to real events: after a trip, after a project or when a shopping decision is finished. You still remember why the pictures exist, so the choices are clearer. Choose one category and one endpoint each time. Keep a short note about deferred items when context is missing. This prevents the same uncertain group from derailing every subsequent session.
If you use iCloud Photos, understand synchronized deletion before taking a larger step. The iCloud guide helps distinguish local storage management from removing items everywhere. The sustainable result is a review habit you are willing to repeat. Keep the photographs you care about, make thoughtful removals, and leave yourself enough attention for the next event rather than trying to reach an arbitrary empty-library target.
Sources and further reading
Apple: Delete or hide photos, iOS 18
Apple: Delete photos on iPhone or iPad
Apple: Check iPhone storage
Questions, answered.
How long should a cleanup session be?
Choose a length or batch you can review attentively. Ten minutes or one familiar event is a useful starting point, then adapt it to your decisions.
Does a left swipe instantly delete a photo in this app?
It marks a removal choice. You can undo or restore an item in the in-app Trash Bin before you confirm deletion.
What should I do with photos I cannot decide about?
Keep them for a later session. Make a note of the missing context and continue with items whose purpose you understand.

Make the choice in three steps
Identify the task. Sorting albums, finding repeated shots, and freeing local storage are different jobs.
Try the built-in Photos collections and inspect Settings → General → iPhone Storage. A cluttered grid does not always mean Photos is your biggest storage problem.
If you need a dedicated review flow, try a small session before committing to a purchase. Check that you can understand what is marked for removal and review it before deletion.
For a personal plan and deliberate swipe decisions, Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete is worth evaluating. For organizing kept photos into albums, Slidebox may be a closer fit. For a detected-duplicates problem alone, Apple Photos may be enough.
Start with the cleanup planner to compare the estimated file bytes in the photos, screenshots, and videos you are considering removing.
Safety applies whichever app you choose
Maintain a separate copy of irreplaceable media. iCloud Photos is a synced library: removing a photo also removes it from other synced devices. Recently Deleted usually provides a 30-day recovery window, unless you permanently remove the item earlier. Keep that window when possible.
Do not choose a cleaner based on claims that it will boost battery life, erase system caches, or guarantee a fixed number of gigabytes. The result depends on your library and what you actually choose to delete.

### How Swipe & Delete Reviews Photos — Methods and Limits
https://swipeanddelete.app/how-it-works.html
Home / Guides
How photo review works—and what it cannot decide for you.
Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete finds photos worth reviewing and helps you make the final choice. Its photo analysis runs on your iPhone; a similarity result is a review suggestion, not proof that two memories are interchangeable.
By Mohamed Elatabany · Updated October 2026 · Suggest a correction
On this page
The review workflow
Similar photos are candidates, not identical files
Photo permission determines the library available for review
iCloud changes availability and storage estimates
Your final confirmation and recovery window
Photo analysis and purchase services
How this explanation is checked
The review workflow
Choose cleanup priorities and a manageable category, such as similar shots, old screenshots, or large videos.
Review the candidates. Swipe right to keep an item and left to mark it for removal.
Undo a swipe or restore marked items from the in-app Trash Bin if you change your mind.
Review your selections and confirm deletion when you are ready.
A storage estimate helps you choose a starting point. It does not mean those bytes are already free, and it does not obligate you to remove anything. The website planner works separately: it calculates from the counts and average sizes you enter and never scans your library.
Similar photos are candidates, not identical files
The app compares visual representations of authorized photos on the device to identify review candidates. Its detection code uses compact signatures from thumbnails and visual feature comparisons. This helps surface repeated compositions without sending your library to a remote scanning service.
A visual comparison has limits. A crop, edit, change in lighting, screenshot, or unusual composition can change a result. Two burst shots can look nearly identical while capturing different expressions. A matching visual signature is not a byte-for-byte comparison of the original files, and a suggested group is not an instruction to delete every item except one.
Inspect faces, text, sharpness, framing, and context before removing a photo. No measured accuracy rate or universal detection guarantee is claimed here. Learn the difference in our similar versus duplicate photos guide.
Photo permission determines the library available for review
The app can analyze only the photos it is authorized to access. Limited access restricts review to the items you have selected for that permission. Photos that are not accessible cannot reliably appear in a scan, even if you can see them elsewhere in Apple Photos.
You control the permission in iPhone Settings. Adjust access if you want to review additional items, and open a small category first to check the result. If an image representation cannot be obtained, a complete comparison may not be possible. An empty result therefore does not prove that your entire library has no similar photos.
iCloud changes availability and storage estimates
With Optimize iPhone Storage enabled, a full-resolution original may be stored in iCloud while your phone holds a smaller local representation. Photo comparison depends on the image data available to the app. A file size displayed for an original is not a promise that deleting it will reclaim the same number of bytes on this phone.
Apple Photos can download iCloud media when you request it. That is separate from uploading your photos to our servers for analysis. The website planner does not know which originals are locally downloaded, so it estimates file bytes rather than guaranteed device space.
Apple explains iCloud Photos and optimized storage. Read our iCloud deletion guide before starting a large cleanup.
Your final confirmation and recovery window
Marking an item in the app and permanently removing a file are different stages. You can restore marked items in the in-app Trash Bin before confirming deletion. After deletion through Photos, Apple normally keeps the item in Recently Deleted for 30 days unless it is permanently removed sooner.
When iCloud Photos is enabled, deletion syncs to other devices using that library. iCloud synchronization is not a separate archive that preserves a deleted item indefinitely. Maintain a separate copy of irreplaceable media and check a backup before relying on it.
Apple’s deletion and recovery instructions explain the recovery window and synced deletion.
Photo analysis and purchase services
Photo analysis happens on the phone. Apple and RevenueCat process purchase services and Pro entitlements, which involve purchase information and app-user identifiers. This distinction matters: on-device analysis does not mean no data is processed by any service.
The app starts with a one-time free allowance. Optional Pro purchases unlock unlimited swipes and advanced cleanup tools. The available options and their current terms appear in the app before purchase. See the privacy information and purchase support.
How this explanation is checked
Written by Mohamed Elatabany, the app’s developer. This explanation was checked against the photo-detection implementation, permission and deletion flows, and the public App Store description on October 4, 2026. It is a product explanation, not an independent laboratory benchmark.
There is no claim that Swipe & Delete is more accurate than Apple Photos or another cleaner. Use the task-based app comparison to decide which workflow fits your needs. Send an incorrect or outdated detail through support, including the page URL and what should be corrected.
Questions, answered.
Does a similar-photo match mean I should delete it?
No. Similarity identifies review candidates. Check each photo and decide which expressions, angles, text, and memories you want to keep.
Can the app compare photos outside my Photos permission?
It can review only authorized, accessible items. Limited access and unavailable image data can limit the candidates shown.
Does a storage estimate equal space already freed?
No. It is an estimate before deletion. Original file size can differ from local device space, especially with Optimize iPhone Storage.
Photo Cleaner: Swipe & Delete is an iPhone photo-cleanup app by Mohamed Elatabany for iOS 17 or later. It offers a personal cleanup plan, duplicate and similar-photo review, screenshot and large-video review, and swipe-to-keep or mark-for-removal controls. Photo analysis happens on your device; photos are not uploaded for scanning. Start with a one-time free allowance; Pro unlocks unlimited swipes and advanced cleanup tools, with subscription and one-time purchase options depending on availability. Rated 5 stars on the US App Store, checked October 4, 2026.
Start free. Pro purchases are optional. Review the current options in the app.
